title: The 4.45x Unit Mismatch That Destroyed NASA's $327.6M Mars Mission
alt_title_1: Pounds vs Newtons: Inside the 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter Handoff Failure
alt_title_2: Why Unchecked Interface Assumptions Wreck Brilliant Engineering
description_hook: On September 23, 1999, NASA lost the $327.6 million Mars Climate Orbiter mission ($125 million spacecraft) because Lockheed Martin ground software output thruster impulse in pound-force seconds while NASA JPL navigation expected metric newton-seconds.

scenes.headline: A $327.6M Mars Mission Lost to a Unit Mismatch
bullets: 286-day journey ended as the $125M probe dipped too low
Two elite aerospace teams assumed different force units
scenes.narration: On September 23, 1999, NASA lost the three-hundred-twenty-seven-point-six-million-dollar Mars Climate Orbiter mission after nine months in deep space because two elite engineering teams used incompatible measurement units.
scenes.source: NASA Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Board Phase I Report (Nov 10, 1999)

scenes.headline: Pound-Force Seconds Met Metric Newton-Seconds
scenes.stat_label: IMPERIAL OUTPUT FED STRAIGHT INTO METRIC NAVIGATION
bullets: Lockheed ground software wrote impulse in pound-force seconds
NASA JPL trajectory code read values as metric newton-seconds
scenes.narration: Lockheed Martin ground software exported thruster impulse in English pound-force seconds while NASA JPL navigation software expected metric newton-seconds, skewing trajectory math by four-point-four-five times and burning up the hundred-twenty-five-million-dollar spacecraft.
scenes.source: NASA Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Board Phase I Report (Nov 10, 1999)

scenes.headline: Modules Pass Internally While Boundaries Fail
scenes.left_body: Bare numbers passed between tools -> hidden 4.45x drift
scenes.right_body: Typed unit keys + end-to-end assertion tests catch mismatches
scenes.narration: Both teams employed world-class engineers whose separate code modules worked internally, yet nobody enforced an automated end-to-end interface test where one system's raw output file became the next system's input.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule based on NASA Mishap Board (1999)

scenes.headline: Name Units in Every Header and Assert Boundaries
scenes.stat_label: EXPLICIT UNIT CONTRACTS PREVENT SILENT DRIFT
scenes.narration: Embed explicit unit names directly into every spreadsheet header, database column, and API key, such as amount_usd_cents or duration_seconds, and validate every external file automatically at the boundary before running downstream math.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin protocol (advice, not a study)

scenes.headline: Audit the Seams Between Your Tools
scenes.stat_label: SYSTEMS BREAK AT SILENT HANDOFFS, NOT INSIDE ONE HEAD
bullets: Never pass unitless numbers across scripts or contractors
Fail loud and immediately when input bounds look off
scenes.narration: Complex operations rarely fail inside one smart specialist's head; they disintegrate at silent handoffs between tools where unit assumptions go completely unchecked.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule based on NASA Mishap Board (1999)
